Will Bitcoin dip to $83,000 on September 27?

post_mortem.what_happened: On Sunday, Sep 27, BTC stayed in a tight range around $84K–$85K as volatility compressed near the end of the quarter, and at one point traded near $84,830. Binance BTC/USDT never touched $83,000, so the market resolved NO.
post_mortem.what_we_missed: The forecast came in at 11:30 AM ET, with only about 12.5 hours left in the window and BTC about 1.5–2% above the strike. It was a quiet weekend with falling volatility, and bitcoin was still drifting up. The market's 7.7% priced that correctly. Our 30% (22% from claude_direct) put too much weight on the Sep 24 dip below $83K, which happened on a weekday during a spike in bond yields.
post_mortem.lesson: For intraday 'dip to X' markets, base the probability on hours remaining, distance to the strike and current realized volatility (weekend volatility is usually lower). Earlier-week tests of a level don't justify a probability 4x the market's.

suggested_change.change: Block large bets that disagree with a crypto touch market by more than 3x unless a simple barrier-hit volatility model (distance to strike, hours left, recent realized vol) supports the forecaster's number.

post_mortem.what_happened: BTC opened Sept 28 near $84,457, then fell to about $83,000 by 7:20am ET and was around $83,069 at 11:35am ET. The drop came from a strong dollar, rising yields and oil, and Trump rejecting Iran's 7-day plan. The noon Binance close was well below $86,000, so the market resolved No.
post_mortem.what_we_missed: The forecaster's newest price reading was from about 16 hours before the judgment. Using it, YES needed a roughly 1.8% rise through the $85,000–$86,000 resistance zone during a week of pullback and yields at 19-year highs. The market priced this at 8.5%, and the forecaster gave 25% without a fresh price or any specific upside catalyst.
post_mortem.lesson: For short-horizon crypto price-threshold markets, get the price at judgment time and estimate the chance of the move from realized volatility. Only move far from the market if you have a concrete catalyst it may be missing.

suggested_change.change: For near-expiry price-threshold questions, block bets that take the opposite side of the market's majority view (e.g. buying YES when the market is below 15%) when the forecast is more than 2x the market price, unless the research includes a price reading from the last 2 hours and a volatility-based probability estimate that supports the gap.

question: Will the price of Bitcoin be above $84,000 on September 28?

post_mortem.what_happened: BTC fell on Sep 28 as the dollar strengthened, bond yields rose and oil climbed after Trump rejected Iran's 7-day plan. It was about $82,958 at 7:20am ET and about $83,069 at 11:35am ET, so the noon Binance candle almost certainly closed below $84,000 and the market resolved NO.
post_mortem.what_worked: Very little, honestly. Our 0.46 was the most bullish number in the room, above jev_alone (0.37), claude_direct (0.32) and the market (0.245). A bold bet sized against a 0.245 price would have been on YES and lost. The research did find the key fact: at judgment time BTC was already about $83,300–83,600, below the strike, after a morning drop. But the forecast leaned on the week's closes near $84.4k instead of the live price and the macro headwinds (10-year yield above 5%).
post_mortem.lesson: For short-horizon price-threshold questions, anchor on the latest timestamped spot price and the distance to the strike in units of typical volatility over the remaining hours, not on the prior week's closes. When the market sits well below 0.5 and spot is already under the strike, explain why the market is wrong before disagreeing with it.

suggested_change.change: Block or shrink bets when the forecast is more than 15 points from the market on a crypto price question with less than 12 hours to resolution, unless the research includes a timestamped spot price that supports the gap.

Both points held up. But a win-only market at 35.5% already made No the favourite, and 8% was much more confident than those facts justify. The unconfirmed '0-0 draw' search snippet was also wrong. suggested_change.change: If a forecast is more than 20 points away from the market price and the research includes an unconfirmed result claim from before the match was played, drop that claim and cap the gap at what the confirmed evidence supports.

question: Will Sweden win on 2026-09-28?

post_mortem.what_happened: Sweden beat Poland 3-1 at Strawberry Arena on 28 September 2026. Nygren scored in the 8th minute, Szymański equalised in the 43rd, and Ayari (63') and Gyökeres (72') won it for Sweden, who now have two wins from two in Nations League B Group 4. Sweden won within 90 minutes, so the market resolved YES.
post_mortem.what_worked: The research took the forecast from 0.35 to 0.55, about 10 points above the market's 0.445. The main reasons were Sweden playing at home, their 5-2 head-to-head record including a 3-2 win at the same ground in March, Poland failing to score against Bosnia, and Poland losing Kaminski. Even so, 55% is close to a coin flip on a result that had three possible outcomes, and Sweden were missing Isak, Holm and Ekdal. The evidence leaned the right way, but the outcome itself was largely luck.
post_mortem.lesson: When a home side has a clear head-to-head record against the same opponent, recent wins at the same venue and better current form, and its opponent is struggling to score, give those facts a few points of weight over the market even if the home side has headline injuries. Their depth may cover the missing players.

suggested_change.change: Before discounting a team for injuries, check who replaces the injured players and whether the team has won without them before (here Nygren, Ayari and Gyökeres covered for Isak), rather than treating a star's absence as a large penalty by default.

Will there be more than 30 transit calls through the Strait of Hormuz from Sep 21, 2026 to Sep 27, 2026? (Above 30)

post_mortem.what_happened: The market resolved NO: IMF PortWatch counted 30 or fewer transit calls through Hormuz for Sep 21–27, 2026. Throughput stayed near 1% of normal after Trump rejected Iran's reopening proposal on Sep 27. PortWatch's Sep 21–27 daily figures were still unpublished in the sources I checked on Sep 29, so I couldn't confirm the exact total. Other trackers reported higher counts because they include dark (AIS-off) transits, e.g. Windward's 24 vessels on Sep 27 and 55 transits over Sep 16–23.
post_mortem.what_worked: The research anchored on PortWatch's own recent numbers: 78 transits over Sep 1–20 (about 27 a week), 8 on Sep 13 and 1 on Sep 20. It also noted that PortWatch is AIS-based and misses dark transits, so it discounted the higher Windward, Reuters and US-official counts. That moved the forecast from 42% without research to 15%, below the market's 20.5%.
post_mortem.lesson: When a question resolves on a specific data source, forecast from that source's recent run rate and how it counts. Treat other trackers' higher figures as noise unless they use the same method, here AIS-visible transits only.

suggested_change.change: For count questions tied to one data provider, always pull that provider's trailing 2–4 week totals and write down its counting rules, such as AIS-only, before looking at other sources.
